extracted.intended_audience: educated early-18th-century reading public interested in literature, manners, and current affairs (Spectator readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical commentary and evaluative criteria for epic poetry (exemplified by close reading of Milton's Paradise Lost, Book I), together with some social-moral prescriptions on domestic behaviour found elsewhere on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper Invocation for Subject
rubrics_metrics.description: His Invocation to a Work which turns in a great measure upon the Creation of the World, is very properly made to the Muse who inspired Moses in those Books from whence our Author drew his Subject, and to the Holy Spirit who is therein represented as operating after a particular manner in the first Production of Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invocation should suit the subject-matter (here the Creation): select an appropriate authority/muse (classical or scriptural) so the opening aligns thematically with the poem's subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainness and Simplicity of Opening Lines
rubrics_metrics.description: These Lines are perhaps as plain, simple and unadorned as any of the whole Poem, in which Particular the Author has conformed himself to the Example of Homer and the Precept of Horace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good epic may begin with clear, unadorned lines; imitating Homer/Horace in restraint at the exordium can be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Transition from Exordium to Fable
rubrics_metrics.description: This whole Exordium rises very happily into noble Language and Sentiment, as I think the Transition to the Fable is exquisitely beautiful and natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The move from invocation/introduction into the poem's narrative (fable) should feel seamless and elevated; abrupt or awkward transitions are faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand and Inventive Circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The Nine Days Astonishment... is a noble Circumstance, and very finely imagined. The Division of Hell into Seas of Fire, and into firm Ground impregnated with the same furious Element, with that particular Circumstance of the Exclusion of Hope from those Infernal Regions, are Instances of the same great and fruitful Invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic poetry should display imaginative large-scale invention in setting and circumstance (world-building, ingenious cosmological/physical details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation through Speech and Action (Satan)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Thoughts in the first Speech and Description of Satan... are wonderfully proper to give us a full Idea of him. His Pride, Envy and Revenge, Obstinacy, Despair and Impenitence, are all of them very artfully interwoven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major characters should be revealed by their speeches and actions in ways that interweave key passions and traits; a first speech can compendiously present a character's composite nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid Physical and Sensory Imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: His being the first that awakens... with his Posture on the burning Lake, his rising from it, and the Description of his Shield and Spear... Thus Satan talking to his nearest Mate, With head up-lift above the wave, and eyes That sparkling blazed...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, sensory detail and striking similes/metaphors to convey physical presence and motion; such imagery raises sublimity and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Sublimity in Person Description
rubrics_metrics.description: But there is no single Passage in the whole Poem worked up to a greater Sublimity, than that wherein his Person is described in those celebrated Lines: --He, above the rest In shape and gesture proudly eminent Stood like a Tower...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for passages where the language attains genuine sublimity in depicting a character's presence; these are high points of epic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between Sentiment and Character
rubrics_metrics.description: His Sentiments are every way answerable to his Character, and suitable to a created Being of the most exalted and most depraved Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A character's expressed sentiments should fit their nature and history; incongruous utterances weaken characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling Impious or Blasphemous Speech as Absurd Rather than Convincing
rubrics_metrics.description: Amidst those Impieties which this Enraged Spirit utters... the Author has taken care to introduce none that is not big with absurdity, and incapable of shocking a Religious Reader; his Words... bearing only a Semblance of Worth, not Substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting impious viewpoints, present them in a way that reveals absurdity rather than endorsing blasphemy; allow readers' moral sensibilities to remain intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex Emotional Depth (e.g., Tears)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor must I here omit that beautiful Circumstance of his bursting out in Tears, upon his Survey of those innumerable Spirits whom he had involved in the same Guilt and Ruin with himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even villainous characters may display complex, poignant emotions; such moments add depth and provoke reflection rather than simple condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learned Allusions and Classical Catalogue Technique
rubrics_metrics.description: The Catalogue of Evil Spirits has abundance of Learning in it, and a very agreeable turn of Poetry, which rises in a great measure from its describing the Places where they were worshipped, by those beautiful Marks of Rivers so frequent among the Ancient Poets. The Author had doubtless in this place Homers Catalogue of Ships, and Virgil's List of Warriors, in his View.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on classical catalogue techniques and erudite allusions (geography, ancient rites) enriches epic texture; such learning should be integrated poetically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshadowing by Character Sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: The Characters of Moloch and Belial prepare the Readers Mind for their respective Speeches and Behaviour in the second and sixth Book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early character sketches should set reader expectations for later actions and speeches—good foreshadowing enhances unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Use of Romantic/Ancient Motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Account of Thammuz is finely Romantick, and suitable to what we read among the Ancients of the Worship which was paid to that Idol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate mythic/romantic motifs when they harmonize with the poem's epic register and echo ancient exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing Plausible Mechanisms for Marvels
rubrics_metrics.description: The Passage in the Catalogue, explaining the manner how Spirits transform themselves by Contractions or Enlargement of their Dimensions, is introduced with great Judgment, to make way for several surprizing Accidents in the Sequel of the Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting supernatural phenomena, supply internally coherent rules or mechanisms so marvelous incidents remain plausible within the poem's logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement in Worldbuilding (ranked distinctions preserved)
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as the Infernal Palace is finished, we are told the Multitude and Rabble of Spirits immediately shrunk themselves into a small Compass... but those of the first Rank and Dignity still preserved their natural Dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish ranks/classes within a supernatural order to create texture and avoid flat uniformity; subtle refinements reward attentive readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Striking Inventive Descriptions of Settings and Objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The Character of Mammon and the Description of the Pandæmonium, are full of Beauties... Azazel's Stature, and of the Infernal Standard... that ghastly Light, by which the Fiends appear to one another in their Place of Torments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose memorable, novel images for key settings/objects (standards, lights, edifices) to make scenes feel singular and awe-inspiring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerful Collective and Martial Imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The Shout of the whole Host of fallen Angels when drawn up in Battel Array... The Review, which the Leader makes of his Infernal Army... He thro the armed files Darts his experienc'd eye, and soon traverse The whole Battalion... Their Number last he sums; and now his Heart Distends with Pride...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use massed action, military review, and collective gestures to convey scale and the emotional tenor of armies or crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic Visual Effects (e.g., flashing swords, artificial illumination)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Flash of Light which appear'd upon the drawing of their Swords... Anon out of the Earth a Fabrick huge Rose like an Exhalation... From the arched Roof Pendent by subtle Magick, many a Row Of Starry Lamps and blazing Crescets, fed With Naphtha and Asphaltus, yielded Light As from a Sky--
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ dynamic visual motifs (light, motion, sudden apparitions) and invented technologies/magics to animate scenes and heighten wonder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended Similes Used to Attain Higher Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When Milton alludes either to Things or Persons, he never quits his Simile till it rises to some very great Idea, which is often foreign to the Occasion that gave Birth to it. The Resemblance ... the Poet runs on with the Hint till he has raised out of it some glorious Image or Sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow similes to develop into extended images that generate high, often expansive ideas; do not truncate a fruitful comparison prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similes as Relief and Diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons... are not introduced only to illustrate and embellish the Discourse, but to amuse and relax the Mind of the Reader, by frequently disengaging him from too painful an Attention to the Principal Subject, and by leading him into other agreeable Images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparisons/similes to vary pace, relieve sustained attention, and introduce auxiliary images that refresh the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Trifling or Over-Nicety in Comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: That it is not necessary in Poetry for the Points of the Comparison to correspond with one another exactly, but that a general Resemblance is sufficient, and that too much Nicety in this Particular favours of the Rhetorician and Epigrammatist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor broad, resonant resemblance in similes rather than pedantic, overly precise correspondences which suggest mere rhetorical cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Episodes, Similes, and Metaphors to Vary the Work
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Reader considers the Conduct of Homer, Virgil and Milton, as the great Fable is the Soul of each Poem, so to give their Works an agreeable Variety, their Episodes are so many short Fables, and their Similes so many short Episodes; to which you may add, if you please, that their Metaphors are so many short Similes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure an epic so the central fable is enlivened by episodic diversions (episodes, long similes, metaphors) that broaden the reader's experience without derailing the main narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to Small Social Trifles to Preserve Affection
rubrics_metrics.description: Emilia's Observation teaches her, that as little Inadvertencies and Neglects cast a Blemish upon a great Character; so the Neglect of Apparel, even among the most intimate Friends, does insensibly lessen their Regards to each other, by creating a Familiarity too low and contemptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In personal/domestic conduct, small attentions (neat apparel, avoiding careless neglect) preserve esteem and reciprocal regard; trifles are consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingenious, Unobtrusive Arts to Please a Spouse
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Help of these, and a thousand other nameless Arts... by the Obstinacy of her Goodness and unprovoked Submission, in spight of all her Afflictions and ill Usage, Bromius is become a Man of Sense and a kind Husband, and Emilia a happy Wife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained, often unspoken practices of kindness, patience, and modest submission can reform and maintain marital affection; such arts are more practised than described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love as a Motive to Self-Improvement and Industry
rubrics_metrics.description: I know not one Motive relating to this Life which would produce so many honourable and worthy Actions, as the Hopes of obtaining a Woman of Merit: There would ten thousand Ways of Industry and honest Ambition be pursued by young Men, who believed that the Persons admired had Value enough for their Passion to attend the Event of their good Fortune in all their Applications...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present love (or the aspiration to win a virtuous partner) as a legitimate incentive for moral self-improvement and industrious behaviour; it's a socially useful motive.
